German uses the same 26 letters as English. What is new is that each letter has its own German name — and you will need those names constantly, because Germans ask you to spell things out loud all the time.
Spelling out loud has its own verb: buchstabieren. Your name, your email, your street — you will spell all of them in your first week in Germany.

And the letters are worth the effort for a second reason: German spells what it says. Learn the sound of each letter and you can read almost any German word correctly on the first try, without a pronunciation guide.
German is written the way it is spoken. Learn the letters once — then you can read almost anything; only eight spellings need learning by hand.

English hides sounds — you cannot tell how through or knight is said just by looking. German does not do that: what is on the page is what comes out of your mouth. So the letters are not just for spelling your name; they are the whole reading system.
Watch three letter names: J = "yot", V = "fow", W = "vay". They are the ones English speakers get wrong most often.

German bilkul jaise likha hai waise hi bola jaata hai — isliye reading aasaan hai. Bas har letter ka naam yaad karo, kyunki apna naam aur email spell karne mein yahi kaam aayega. Teen letters dhyaan se: J = "yot", V = "fow", W = "vay".
J-V-W = "yot–fow–vay". Teen naam, ek saans mein. Baaki alphabet English jaisa hi hai.
Same 26 letters as English — only the names are new.
German spells what it says: sounds → reading, no guessing.
The three traps are J "yot", V "fow", W "vay".

On the phone, at a bank, at a government office — just saying "B" is often not clear enough, because B and P (or D and T) sound almost the same down a phone line. So Germans anchor each letter to a word: A wie Apfel ("A as in Apfel").

You will hear this every single time you give your name or address over the phone, and you are expected to do it back. There is no fixed official list you must memorise — any well-known word works, so use the vocabulary you already have.
Letter + wie + Word beginning with that letter
A wie Apfel · B wie Buch · H wie Hund
A wie Apfel, B wie Buch, H wie Hund.
Weber — mit W, nicht mit V.
Z wie Zeit, S wie Schule, K wie Käse.

Phone par sirf letter ka naam bolne se confusion hoti hai (B aur P, D aur T ek jaise sunte hain). Isliye Germans letter ke saath ek word bolte hain: A wie Apfel = "A jaisa Apfel mein". Koi official list nahi hai — jo word aata ho, wahi bol do.
Frau Weber does exactly this when she says Weber, mit W — she is clearing up W vs V before Rohan writes it down wrong.
The umlauts (ä ö ü) and the ß
Beyond A–Z German has four extra signs. Three are umlauts — a vowel with two dots, which changes the sound — and one is the ß (Eszett), a sharp "ss".
These are not decoration. Umlaut dots change the word: Mutter is "mother", Mütter is "mothers". Drop the dots and you have said something else.
The dots are part of the letter, not an accent you may leave off. If you cannot type them, write ae oe ue ss — never bare a o u s.
like "e" in bed — long in Käse, short in Äpfel
lips rounded as for "o", but say "e"
lips rounded as for "u", but say "ee"
one sharp, voiceless "ss" — never a "z" sound

Two facts about ß: it never starts a word, and it only appears after a long vowel (Straße, Fuß) or a vowel pair like ei / au (heißen, weiß, außen). After a short vowel German writes ss instead: Fluss, müssen. Saying them out loud: ä = "A-Umlaut", ö = "O-Umlaut", ü = "U-Umlaut", ß = "Eszett" (or "scharfes S"). So Käse is spelled "kah – A-Umlaut – ess – ay".

Char extra signs hain: ä ö ü (do dots = umlaut) aur ß (sharp "ss"). ö aur ü ka trick: honth "o"/"u" ke shape mein rakho, par andar se "e"/"ee" bolo. Dots optional nahi hain — Mutter (maa) aur Mütter (maayein) do alag words hain. Type na kar pao to ae oe ue ss likho.
Umlaut ka formula: honth pehle wale vowel ke, aawaaz "e" family ki — ö = honth O + "e", ü = honth U + "ee", ä = seedha "e". Aur ß vs ss: lamba vowel → ß, chhota vowel → ss.
ä ö ü change the meaning — the dots are not optional.
ß = sharp "ss"; it never begins a word.
Long vowel or vowel pair → ß. Short vowel → ss.
Eight sound rules beginners always mix up
Eight spellings do not sound the way an English reader expects. These eight cause almost every beginner mispronunciation — fix them now and you will read German aloud with confidence.
Seven of the eight are completely regular — the spelling always makes the same sound. Only v has a second setting, and it is easy to spot.
Two moves cover almost all of it: in ei/ie say the second vowel, and at the start of a word the s-family softens — s = "z", st = "sht", sp = "shp".
Say the second vowel: Eis = "ice", mein = "mine".
ei is a spelling pair, not a word: it sounds like the English word "eye".
ei is a spelling pair, not a word: it sounds like the English word "eye".
Again the second vowel: Liebe = "LEE-buh", vier = "feer".
ie is a spelling pair, not a word: read the second vowel, so it sounds like "ee".
ie is a spelling pair, not a word: read the second vowel, so it sounds like "ee".
sch is a spelling group, not a word: it is the English "sh".
sch is a spelling group, not a word: it is the English "sh".

In old German words v is always "f": Vater = "FAH-ter", vier = "feer", von, viel. ⚠️ One exception: in words German borrowed from other languages, v keeps its "v" sound — Video ("VEE-day-oh"), Vase, Klavier, November. If the word looks international, say "v".
w is the English "v": Wasser = "VA-ser", wie = "vee". German has no English "w" sound at all.
s → "z" (at the start of a word)
sagen = "ZAH-gen", sieben = "ZEE-ben", Sonne = "ZO-nuh". Between two vowels too: Käse = "KAY-zuh". But a double ss stays sharp: Wasser = "VA-ser".
At the start of a word st = "sht" and sp = "shp": Straße = "SHTRAH-suh", Stift = "shtift", Sport = "shport". That is why buchstabieren sounds like "BOOKH-shta-BEE-ren".

Ye rules yaad rakhne hi padenge, par logic simple hai: German mein ek spelling aksar ek hi tarah boli jaati hai — English ki tarah har word ka guess nahi karna padta. ei = "eye" (Eis = ice), ie = "ee" (Liebe = LEE-buh), z = "ts" (Zeit = TSAIT), sch = English "sh" (Schule = SHOO-luh), v = "f" (Vater = FAH-ter), w = "v" (Wasser = VA-ser), aur shuru ka s = "z" (sagen = ZAH-gen), st- = "sht" (Straße = SHTRAH-suh). Sirf v ka ek exception hai: international words mein v = "v" hi rehta hai (Video, Vase).
ei/ie — doosra vowel bolo. v aur w ek step aage khisak jaate hain: v se f, w se v. Aur shuru mein s soft ho jaata hai: s se z, st se sht.
ei = "eye", ie = "ee" — always the second vowel.
v = "f", w = "v" — except in international words, where v stays "v".

a1-10-artikel: Every German noun has a gender — der (m), die (f) or das (n) — and the article is part of the word. Learn the patterns that hint at gender, the one habit that saves you years of mistakes, and how plural turns almost everything into die.
Never learn a German noun alone — learn it with its article. Not Tisch but der Tisch; not Straße but die Straße. The colour of the article (der/die/das) is the gender, and you carry it for life.

der · die · das — the three genders
Gender is a property of the word, not of the thing. So you learn it with the word, not by thinking about the thing.

Hindi has grammatical gender too, and it does not always match reality either. German simply has three boxes instead of two — and like Hindi, the box was decided centuries before anyone asked whether it made sense.
Gender cheez ka nahi, shabd ka hai. Isliye sochna nahi, saath yaad karna hai.
Every German Nomen (noun) has a gender, shown by its Artikel (article). There are three, and English has none of them — so this is new territory.
The article is not optional decoration: it is part of the word. der = masculine, die = feminine, das = neuter.
Gender is rarely logical — das Mädchen (girl) is neuter! That is why you memorise the article with the noun, not the noun alone.

Har German Nomen (noun) ka ek gender hota hai, jo Artikel dikhata hai: der (maskulin), die (feminin), das (neutrum). Hindi/English jaisa logic mat lagao — das Mädchen (ladki) neutrum hai! Isliye article ko noun ka hissa samjho. Sirf noun yaad karoge to aadha kaam hi hoga, aur baad mein wahi galti banta hai.
The golden rule: learn the article WITH the noun
Never store a noun alone. der Tisch is the word; Tisch is half a word.
Article noun ka surname hai — akela naam adhoora hai.
Colour or group your words by article, not alphabetically.
A flashcard without an article will teach you wrong German.
The single best habit in all of A1: never write a noun without its colour. Build the article into the word from day one.
Use an Assoziation (association): picture der Tisch in blue, die Straße in green, das Buch in orange. A Mindmap by colour beats a plain list.
On your flashcards (Lernkarten from Chapter 9), always write the article. A card that says just "Tisch" is a card that will teach you the wrong German.

A1 ki sabse achhi aadat: noun kabhi article ke bina mat likho. Pehle din se article andar build karo. Assoziation use karo — der Tisch ko neela, die Straße ko hara, das Buch ko orange socho. Plain list se Mindmap behtar hai. Lernkarte par hamesha article likho — bina article wala card tumhe galat German sikha dega.
Endings give you good guesses, not guarantees — except -chen and -lein, which are always neuter.
Sirf ek pakka rule: -chen / -lein = das. Baaki sab andaaza hai, aur andaaza bhi kaafi kaam ka hai.
Gender is mostly unpredictable, but some Wortenden (word endings) give strong hints. These are tendencies, not laws — but they help you guess well.
The -chen/-lein rule is the one that never breaks: those words are always neuter, whatever they mean.

Gender zyadatar unpredictable hai, par kuch Wortenden (word endings) hint dete hain: -e aksar feminin (die Karte), -ung/-heit/-tion feminin, -chen/-lein hamesha neutrum (das Würstchen), -er (karne wala/tool) aksar maskulin. Yeh tendencies hain, pakke rule sirf -chen/-lein.
ein / eine, and the plural die
Masculine and neuter share ein; only feminine adds -e. And every plural is die.
Plural mein gender ki tension khatam — sab die lete hain. Yeh A1 ka sabse easy rule hai.
ein for masculine and neuter, eine for feminine.
Plural is die for every gender.
No indefinite article exists in the plural.
Besides the bestimmt (definite) der/die/das, there is the unbestimmt (indefinite) ein/eine — English a/an. It follows gender too.
And the good news about the Plural: in the plural, every noun takes die, no matter its singular gender.
Note masculine and neuter share ein; only feminine adds the -e → eine. And plural is always die — one easy win.

Definite (bestimmt) der/die/das ke alawa indefinite (unbestimmt) ein/eine bhi hai (a/an). Maskulin aur neutrum dono ein; feminin mein eine. Achhi khabar: Plural mein har noun die leta hai — chahe singular ka gender kuch bhi ho. Yeh ek easy win hai.
Four habits, and the first one is the most expensive: every noun you learn without its article is a word you will get wrong later.

Two ways to say no: kein vs nicht
Crossing out a noun? kein. Crossing out anything else? nicht.

German negates the article rather than the sentence: ein Buch becomes kein Buch, one word replacing another. English cannot do this, which is why "not a book" feels like the natural translation and produces the classic mistake nicht ein Buch.
Pehle poochho: main noun ko negate kar raha hoon ya kisi aur cheez ko? Noun ho to kein, baaki sab mein nicht.
kein replaces the article in front of a noun.
nicht handles verbs, adjectives and whole statements.
nicht ein never exists — it is always kein.
German has two negators, and the choice is simple once you see it. kein negates a noun; nicht negates everything else.
Ask yourself: am I crossing out a thing (a noun)? Use kein. Crossing out an action, a quality, or a whole statement? Use nicht.
kein is literally the "not-a" — it is called the Negationsartikel because it replaces ein/the article in front of a noun.

Do negator: kein noun ke liye, nicht baaki sab ke liye. Khud se poochho — kya main koi cheez yaani noun ko negate kar raha hoon? To kein aayega (kein Buch). Aur agar action, quality ya poori baat ko negate kar raha hoon, to nicht (nicht müde, kommt nicht). kein ko Negationsartikel kehte hain — yeh ein/article ki jagah aata hai.
kein = ein + k. Whatever ending ein would take, kein takes too.
ein ke aage k lagao, aur ending wahi rakho. Naya kuch yaad nahi karna.
Because kein stands where the article goes, it takes the same endings as ein (from Chapter 10). Gender and case decide the ending.
For now, the two you will use most are kein (m/n) and keine (f/pl). The masculine object form keinen comes back in the next chapter, Akkusativ.

kein wahi endings leta hai jo ein (Chapter 10). Gender aur case se ending tay hoti hai: feminine keine (keine Zeit), masc./neuter kein (kein Tisch, kein Buch), masc. object keinen (keinen Stift), plural keine. Abhi sabse zyada kein aur keine use hoga.
Negating the whole sentence → nicht at the end. Negating one word → nicht right in front of it.
Poori baat ko "nahi" karna hai? To nicht sentence ke end mein. Sirf ek word ko? To nicht us word se pehle.
One word → nicht immediately before it.
nicht mehr = not anymore; kein … mehr = no more (of a noun).
A few simple placements cover most A1 sentences. nicht sits at the end of a short sentence, or directly before the adjective/adverb/place it negates.
Two handy pairs: nicht mehr = not anymore (for verbs/adjectives), and kein … mehr = no more (for nouns): keine Zeit mehr.

Aasaan placement: nicht chhote sentence ke end mein (Er kommt nicht), ya jis adjective ya place ko negate karna hai uske theek pehle (nicht müde, nicht hier). Do useful: nicht mehr (ab nahi — verb/adjective) aur kein … mehr (aur nahi — noun): keine Zeit mehr.

a1-12-akkusativ: The accusative is the case of the direct object — the thing a verb acts on. The good news: only one thing changes. Masculine der becomes den (and ein becomes einen); die, das and plural die stay exactly the same.

German marks the object on the article, not by position. That is why Den Mann sehe ich still means "I see the man" even though the man comes first — the den has already told you who is being seen. English has no way to do this, so it relies on word order instead.
Verb ke baad Wen? poochho — jo jawaab aaye, wahi Akkusativ.
Most sentences have three parts: who does it (the subject, in the Nominativ), the action (the verb), and what it is done to (the direct object, in the Akkusativ).
Find the object by asking Wen? (whom?) for a person or Was? (what?) for a thing, after the verb.
The subject does the action; the object receives it. "Ich sehe den Mann" — I (subject) see the man (object). Ask Wen sehe ich? → den Mann.

Zyadatar sentence mein teen hisse: subject (kaun — Nominativ), verb (action), aur object (kis par — Akkusativ). Object dhoondhne ke liye verb ke baad Wen? (kisko) ya Was? (kya) poochho. Subject action karta hai, aur object us action ko receive karta hai.
Only the masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen. Feminine, neuter and plural do not move at all.
m: der Mann → den Mann · ein → einen
f: die Karte → die Karte (no change)
n: das Buch → das Buch (no change)
pl: die Bücher → die Bücher (no change)
Chaar gender mein se teen bilkul same rehte hain. Bas masculine par dhyaan do: der → den.
The whole accusative for A1 is der → den and ein → einen.

kein → keinen follows the same masculine rule.
Here is the whole accusative in one line: only the masculine article changes. Feminine, neuter and plural look exactly the same as the nominative.
The indefinite article matches: masculine ein → einen (Ich habe einen Stift); feminine eine and neuter ein stay. And kein → keinen (m) from Chapter 11.

Poora Akkusativ ek line mein: sirf masculine article badalta hai — der → den (den Mann). Feminine (die), neuter (das), plural (die) bilkul same rehte hain. Indefinite bhi: ein → einen (einen Stift); eine/ein same. Aur kein → keinen (Chapter 11).
If the verb can be followed by "…what?", it takes an accusative object.
Verb aur object ko hamesha ek saath practice karo — einen Stift haben, den Schlüssel suchen — taaki case sochna na pade.
Many everyday verbs are followed by a direct object in the accusative. Learn the verb together with "… + object" so the case comes automatically.
haben, sehen, suchen, finden, kaufen, brauchen, essen, trinken, lesen — all take an object in the accusative.

The gift: no adjective endings here
After sein, the adjective takes no ending at all — whatever the gender or number.

The ending on a German adjective exists to point at the noun that follows it. After sein there is no following noun — the adjective is describing backwards, at the subject — so there is nothing to point at and no ending to add.

After sein, the adjective takes no ending at all — it stays exactly as in the dictionary, whatever the gender or number of the subject.

sein, haben, werden — the big three
Three verbs, and all three misbehave only in du and er/sie/es — except sein, which misbehaves everywhere.
haben du aur er mein apna "b" gira deta hai: hast, hat. werden mein "e" badal kar "i" ho jaata hai: wirst, wird. Aur sein ka koi logic nahi hai — use bas yaad karna padta hai.
Three irregular verbs power most A1 German. sein (to be) is fully irregular; haben (to have) and werden (to become) only wobble in du and er/sie/es.
Learn these by heart — they appear in almost every sentence. sein is the most irregular German verb; haben drops the b in du hast / er hat; werden gives du wirst / er wird.

Teen sabse zaroori irregular verbs: sein (hona) poora irregular hai; haben (paas hona) du/er mein "b" gira deta hai (du hast, er hat); werden (banna) → du wirst, er wird. Inhe bas yaad karna padta hai.

German word order has one golden rule: the conjugated verb is always in position 2. Start with the subject (Ich lerne abends Deutsch) or start with a time word (Abends lerne ich Deutsch) — either way the verb stays second, and the subject simply hops behind it.

The golden rule — verb in position 2
Slot 1 holds one idea (any length). Slot 2 holds the verb. Nothing negotiates.
Slot 1 ek idea hai, ek shabd nahi — "Am Nachmittag" teen shabd hain par ek hi seat leta hai.
In every German statement, the conjugated verb sits in position 2. Position 1 can be the subject OR a time word OR a place — but slot 2 is reserved for the verb.
One shape breaks this, and only one: the yes/no question, where the verb moves to position 1 instead. The third block below puts the two side by side.
Count to the verb: whatever is in slot 1, the verb is slot 2. "Position 1" counts as ONE block, even if it’s several words ("Am Nachmittag").

Sabse zaroori rule yeh hai: normal statement mein conjugated verb position 2 par hota hai. Sirf Ja/Nein sawaal alag hai, jahan verb position 1 par chala jaata hai — woh neeche teesre block mein dikhaya hai. Baaki har case mein position 1 par kuch bhi ho — subject, time word ya place — slot 2 verb ka hi rehta hai. Aur dhyaan rakho ki position 1 ek poora block hota hai, chahe usme do-teen words ho jaayein, jaise "Am Nachmittag".
Inversion — front a time word, flip the subject
The verb never moves. If something else takes slot 1, the subject is what gets displaced.

When you start with something other than the subject (usually a time word), the subject jumps to right after the verb. This is called inversion.
The verb does NOT move — it stays in position 2. Only the subject hops behind it: Morgens dusche ich, never "Morgens ich dusche".

Jab sentence subject ke alawa kisi cheez se shuru ho (aksar time word), to subject verb ke turant baad aata hai. Verb hilta nahi — position 2 pe hi rehta hai: Morgens dusche ich, "Morgens ich dusche" galat hai.

At the start of the word you hear the first sound.
Am Silbenanfang steht oft ein Konsonant.

Im Wortinneren ist der Vokal oft kurz.

Pay attention to the long vowels!
a und aa klingen gleich, aber aa ist lang.
a and aa sound the same, but aa is long.
Ein doppelter Konsonant macht den Vokal kurz.

The five vowels — a · e · i · o · u

German has the same five vowel letters as English, but each one makes a single, clean sound. English slides one vowel into another — "no" is really "no-oo". German does not slide. You set the mouth, make the sound, stop.
Every one of these five comes in a long and a short version, and the next block shows how to tell which. The table below gives you both, so your ear has the pair from the start.
One vowel letter, one mouth position. Do not let the sound drift while you say it.
Hindi works the same way — a in "kal" is one steady sound. So this is a habit you already have; you only have to stop importing the English slide.
An unstressed e at the end of a word is neither long nor short — it relaxes into a soft "uh": Schule = "SHOO-luh", Käse = "KAY-zuh". You will hear this ending on hundreds of words.

German ke vowels saaf aur single hote hain — English ki tarah fisalte nahi. Hindi bhi aise hi chalti hai, to yeh aadat tumhare paas already hai; bas English wala kheenchna band karna hai. Har vowel do lambaai mein aata hai — chhota aur lamba — aur dono ko jodi mein sunna sabse tez tareeka hai: Apfel / Jahr, Kind / Liebe, Mund / Buch.
Vowel ko ek jagah pakad ke rakho — muh hile to sound English ban gaya.
Five vowel letters, each one clean sound — no sliding.
Every vowel has a short and a long version; learn them as pairs.
Unstressed -e at the end = soft "uh" (Schule, Käse).
Chapter 1 gave you the letter names and the traps (z = "ts", w = "v", s- = "z"). This chapter is about the vowels inside the words those letters spell.
Long vs short — the spelling tells you
You never have to guess a vowel's length. German writes the answer into the spelling: look at what follows the vowel, and you know whether to hold it or snap it.
This one signal fixes more beginner pronunciation than anything else in the chapter, because length is what makes Stadt (city) different from Staat (state).
Crowded after the vowel → short. Roomy after the vowel → long.

Think of the vowel as having a room. Two consonants crowd in and squeeze it short. A single consonant, a doubled vowel or a silent h leaves space, so the vowel stretches out. The spelling is a map of that room.
double vowel (aa ee oo) → LONG (Haar, See)

⚠️ Two limits, and they are both easy. First, the rule describes the stressed syllable — unstressed vowels are always relaxed and short. Second, a handful of very common little words break it and are simply short: das, was, mit, hat, es, bin, bis. You will use them so often that they learn themselves.

Length guess karne ki zarurat nahi — spelling bata deti hai. Vowel ke baad do consonant ho to vowel chhota ho jaata hai (Mann, ist). Aur jagah ho — ek consonant, double vowel, ya silent h — to vowel lamba (gut, Haar, Jahr). Yeh farak matlab badal deta hai: Stadt (shehar) vs Staat (rajya). Do chhoti limits: rule stressed syllable par lagta hai, aur kuch rozmarra ke chhote words (das, was, mit, hat, es) hamesha chhote hain.
Vowel ke baad do consonant = chhota, ek consonant = lamba. Ek hi cheez dekhni hai: baad mein kitne consonant hain.
Two or more consonants after the vowel → short.
One consonant, a doubled vowel, or a silent h → long.
a and aa are the same sound — aa is just the long one (Stadt / Staat).
Only the stressed syllable follows the rule; a few tiny words (das, mit, was) are just short.
Vowel pairs — ei · ie · au · eu
Two vowel letters standing together are not two sounds. Each pair is one fixed sound, and there are only four pairs to know.
These four are completely regular — no exceptions to learn. Once you can see a pair and say its sound without thinking, most German words are readable on sight.
In ei and ie, say the second letter. au = "ow", eu = "oy".
This is why Aussprache starts with an "ow" sound: Au-sprache = "OWS-shprah-khuh". When you see it written AUS-spra-che, that is marking the stress, not the sound.

Do vowel saath khade ho to woh ek sound hai, do nahi. Sirf chaar jodi hain: ei = "eye" (Eis), ie = "ee" (Liebe), au = "ow" (laut), eu/äu = "oy" (heute). ei aur ie ka faisla aasaan — doosra letter bolo. Inme koi exception nahi, isliye ek baar pakad liya to permanent hai.
ei/ie — doosra letter bolo. au = "ow" jaise "now", eu = "oy" jaise "boy".
Four pairs, one sound each, zero exceptions.
ei = "eye", ie = "ee" — the second letter wins.
You already met ei and ie in Chapter 1 as reading traps. Here they join their two missing partners, au and eu, so the set is complete.
Two dots on a vowel make a new sound. ä is easy for you — it is just "e". ö and ü are the two German sounds that exist in neither Hindi nor English, so they need a minute of mouth-training.
The training trick works because these sounds are literally a mix: the lips of one vowel with the tongue of another. Set the lips first, then say the other vowel without moving them.
For ö and ü: lips of "o"/"u", sound of "e"/"ee". Lips stay still.
just "e" in bed, held or snapped
The length rule from the last block still applies here: Käse has one consonant after the ä, so it is long; München has two, so the ü is snapped short.

Do dots = umlaut. ä bilkul "e" jaisa hai — yeh aasaan wala hai. ö aur ü Hindi mein nahi hain, isliye trick yaad rakho: honth "o"/"u" ke shape mein set karo, phir bina hilaye "e"/"ee" bolo. Honth hil gaye to sound wapas purana ho jaayega. Aur length ka rule inpar bhi lagta hai: Käse lamba, München chhota.
Honth ek vowel ke, aawaaz doosre vowel ki. ö = honth O + "e". ü = honth U + "ee". ä = seedha "e".
ä = "e". No new mouth position needed.
ö = lips "o" + sound "e". ü = lips "u" + sound "ee".
Umlauts obey the same long/short spelling rule as plain vowels.
Three consonant habits: ch · -ig · final d/g/b
The vowels are the hard part; these three consonant habits are the rest. Each one shows up in almost every German sentence, including every sentence in this chapter.
ch has two sounds and the vowel in front of it decides which — you do not choose. -ig at the end of a word is a fixed ending. And a d, g or b at the end of a word hardens.
After a, o, u → ch is throaty "kh". After i, e and the umlauts → ch is soft, like a whispered "hy". Word-final -ig = "ikh".
a / o / u + ch → throaty "kh" (Buch, noch, achten)
i / e / ä ö ü + ch → soft "hy" (ich, München, Mädchen)
word-final d / g / b → t / k / p (und, Tag, halb)
ch after i e ä ö ü

The final-consonant hardening only happens at the end of a word or syllable. Put a vowel after it and the soft sound comes back: Tag is "tahk", but Tage is "TAH-guh"; Hund is "hunt", but Hunde is "HUN-duh".

Teen consonant rules hain, aur teeno har German sentence mein aate hain. ch ka sound uske pehle wale vowel se tay hota hai — tumhe choose nahi karna padta: a/o/u ke baad gale se "kh" (Buch, noch), aur i/e/umlaut ke baad halka "hy" (ich, München). Word ke end mein -ig = "ikh" (wichtig). Aur end ka d/g/b sakht ho jaata hai — t/k/p (und = "unt", sag = "zahk") — kyunki word khatam hote waqt aawaaz band ho jaati hai. Vowel lagao to soft wapas: Tag = "tahk", par Tage = "TAH-guh".
ch ka sound uske aage wala vowel decide karta hai: mota vowel (a o u) = mota kh, patla vowel (i e ä ö ü) = patla hy. Aur word ke end mein d/g/b sakht ho jaate hain.
ch: throaty after a o u, soft after i e ä ö ü.
Final d g b harden to t k p — but only at the end.
Chapter 1 promised these two: ch and -ig. That is why Mädchen was written "MAYT-khen" there — now you know which of the two ch sounds it is, and why.
Stress & the music of a word

One syllable in every word is betont — stressed: a little louder, longer and clearer than the others. Put the stress on the wrong syllable and a correctly pronounced word can still be hard to understand.
In German the stress is almost always the first syllable. Two things move it, and both are predictable.
Stress the first syllable — unless the word starts with an unstressed prefix (be- ge- ver- er- ent-), or it is an obvious international word.
normal German word → FIRST syllable (AP-fel, AUS-spra-che)
be- / ge- / ver- / er- → skip the prefix (be-TO-nung, ver-STE-hen)
international word → usually the end (Mu-SIK, Stu-DENT, Ho-TEL)
be- is an unstressed prefix, so the stress moves past it
borrowed word — stress at the end

Across a whole sentence the pitch also moves — the Satzmelodie. It falls at the end of a statement and rises at the end of a yes/no question. Same words, different melody, different meaning: Du kommst. / Du kommst?

Har word mein ek syllable betont hoti hai, matlab uspar thoda zyada zor padta hai aur woh thodi lambi bolti jaati hai. German mein aksar pehli syllable par zor hota hai, jaise AP-fel aur AUS-spra-che. Do cheezein ise hila deti hain, aur dono predictable hain. Pehli, be-, ge-, ver-, er- aur ent- prefix par zor nahi padta, isliye be-TO-nung bolte hain — yeh koi borrowed word nahi hai, bas prefix skip ho raha hai. Doosri, bahar se aaye words ka zor aakhir mein hota hai, jaise Mu-SIK. Class mein ek trick kaam karti hai: stressed syllable par mez klopfen karo, aur haath tumhare kaan ko sikha dega.
Zor pehli syllable par — jab tak be-/ge-/ver-/er- saamne na ho. Prefix ko skip karo, phir pehli syllable.
German stress = first syllable, as a default.
Unstressed prefixes be- ge- ver- er- ent- get skipped (be-TO-nung).
International words usually stress the end (Mu-SIK).
Statement falls at the end; yes/no question rises.
Four habits carry over from Hindi and English. None of them are hard to fix — they are just automatic, so you have to catch them once and then listen for them.
Each one below is a real rule from this chapter, seen from the wrong side.
The double n crowds the vowel, so the a is snapped short. Crowded = short.
German j is the English "y", and the silent h gives the a room to stretch.
ü is not "oo". Set the lips, then change only the sound — not the lips.
A d at the end of a word hardens to t. Add a vowel and it softens again: Hunde = "HUN-duh".

Chaar aadat Hindi aur English se aa jaati hain, aur ek baar inhe pakad lo to phir tum khud hi notice karne lagoge. Mann mein chhota "man" bolna hai, kyunki double n ne vowel ko daba diya hai. Jahr ko "yaar" bolo, kyunki German ka j "y" ki tarah bolta hai. über mein ü ko "oo" nahi bolna — honth gol karke "ee" bolo. Aur word ke end ka -d, -g ya -b sakht ho jaata hai: Hund = "hunt" aur Tag = "tahk".
Chaar check: length theek? j ko "y" bola? ü par honth gol? end ka d/g/b sakht?
Chapter 3 (Zahlen 0–100) is your first real test of all this — German numbers are full of short vowels, ei, z and word-final -g: zwei, drei, zwanzig, dreißig.
Feminine nouns take die in the nominative.
The thing being described — subject in the nominative. Stress falls on AUS.
From sein (to be). Short i — two consonants follow.
Note: w = "v", and final -ig sounds like "ikh".
Command form of sprechen. sch = "sh", short i.
Short a (two consonants), then long a. s sounds like "z".
au is one sound, like "ow" in now.
Command form of achten. ch after a = throaty "kh".
au = "ow". Goes with achten auf = pay attention to.
Plural article — here before Betonung group.
The thing to attend to — object. Stress on the long second syllable: be-TOH-nung.
Command form again — now with a separable prefix coming.
Prefix of nachsprechen — it jumps to the end: "Sprich … nach".
Command form of sagen. s = "z", final g → "k".
ch after o = throaty "kh". Part of noch einmal.
Pronunciation is important. Speak slowly and aloud. Pay attention to the stress. Repeat after me and say it once more.
Jonas, morgen sprichst du über deine Stadt. Sag "München" bitte langsam.
Jonas, tomorrow you talk about your city. Please say "Munich" slowly.
Gut, aber höre den Umlaut: Mün-chen. Noch einmal.
Good, but listen to the umlaut: Mün-chen. Once more.
München! Jetzt hört es sich besser an.
Jonas, morgen sprichst du über deine Stadt. Sag "München" bitte langsam. München. Gut, aber höre den Umlaut: Mün-chen. Noch einmal. München! Jetzt hört es sich besser an.
Jonas, tomorrow you talk about your city. Please say "Munich" slowly. Munich. Good, but listen to the umlaut: Mün-chen. Once more. Munich! Now it sounds better.
Für eine Präsentation über seine Stadt
"Morgen sprichst du über deine Stadt" — he is preparing to talk about his city.
Which sound does Frau Bauer correct?
"Höre den Umlaut: Mün-chen" — she is correcting the ü sound.
Die Lehrerin sagt: Sprich bitte langsam nach — München.
The teacher says: repeat slowly after me — München.
Deine Lehrerin fragt: Wo ist die Betonung in „Aussprache“?
Your teacher asks: where is the stress in “Aussprache”?
Die Betonung ist am Wortanfang: AUS-sprache.
The stress is at the start of the word: AUS-sprache.
Dein Partner spricht zu schnell. Was sagst du ihm?
Your partner speaks too fast. What do you say to him?
Sprich bitte langsam und laut. Noch einmal!
Please speak slowly and loudly. Once more!
Write three words from this chapter. For each, mark the vowel as long or short and underline the stressed syllable (e.g. "Mann — short a — MANN"). Use the coaching words if you can.
In which word is the vowel SHORT?
Mann has a double n → the a is short. The others are long (silent h, single consonant, double vowel).
A typical classroom instruction: "Sprich langsam und laut." — Speak slowly and aloud.
Match each umlaut/sound to how you make it.
A double consonant (e.g. "nn" in Mann) tells you the vowel is…
A doppelt (double) consonant shortens the vowel before it: Mann = short a.
How do you make the German "ü" (as in über)?
Round your lips for "oo", then say "ee" without moving them.
Where does German word stress usually fall?
Most native German words are stressed on the first syllable: AP-fel, AUS-spra-che.
The vowels "a" and "aa" (as in Stadt vs Staat)…
sound the same — aa is just longer
a and aa are the same vowel quality; aa is simply the long version. (gleich = the same.)
j = "y" and the silent h makes the a long: "yaar".
German vowels are pure and single, and come in two lengths — the spelling tells you long or short.
Three umlauts: ä ("e"), ö and ü (round the lips, then "e"/"ee").
Stress is usually the first syllable; klopfen (tap) it out to train your ear.
Say minimal pairs aloud daily: Mann/Bahn, Stadt/Staat — feel the short vs long.

a1-20-modalverben1: Modal verbs let you say what you can, must, want and would like to do. Meet können, müssen, wollen and möchten — and the one structural trick behind them all: the modal sits in position 2 and the main verb jumps to the very end (the Satzklammer).

A party is coming. Jule wants to plan it, Finn definitely wants to come, and Finn must finish his homework first. As they sort out who can do what, every sentence shows the same shape — modal in position 2, main verb at the very end.
Every word in every line is clickable
Hear the modal + infinitive "bracket" in real speech
Finn, tomorrow we are having a party. Are you coming?
Finn, kal hum party kar rahe hain. Tum aaoge?
The modal sends the infinitive to the end (this chapter).
Sure! I would like to come. What can I do?
Bilkul! Main khushi se aana chahta hoon. Main kya kar sakta hoon?
You can do the music. We still have to plan the food.
Tum music kar sakte ho. Hamein abhi khaane ki planning karni hai.
möchten = would like — the polite wish (this chapter).
I would like to eat pizza.
I would like to eat pizza. Can we order pizza?
Main pizza khaana chahta hoon. Kya hum pizza order kar sakte hain?
Yes, we can do that. But then you have to pay!
Haan, hum yeh kar sakte hain. Par phir tumhein paise dene honge!
Hmm. Then I only want to eat one piece!
Hmm. Toh main sirf ek tukda khaana chahta hoon!
Typical! Okay, I will order the pizza. You do the music.
Bilkul tumhaare jaisa! Theek hai, main pizza order karungi. Tum music karo.

A modal verb pairs with a second verb to say what you can, must, want or would like to do. The structure never changes: the modal takes position 2, and the main verb — always an infinitive — jumps to the very end. Ich muss heute Deutsch lernen.

You are a warm, encouraging German (A1) tutor for a Hindi/English-speaking beginner. The lesson is MODAL VERBS 1: können (can/ability), müssen (must/necessity), wollen (want/intention), and möchten (would like/polite wish). The learner wrote sentences using modal verbs below. können / müssen / wollen / möchten, full conjugation tables, the Satzklammer, and Hindi-speaker notes.
Say what you want to do
Make a polite wish or request
Send the main verb to the end
We want to have a party.
The verb is at the end of the sentence.
Modalverb und Infinitiv bilden die Satzklammer.
Modal and infinitive form the sentence bracket.
A modal never works alone — it always brings a second verb, and that second verb goes to the end.
Modal batata hai ki kaam kaisa hai — zaroori hai, possible hai, ya tum chahte ho. Asli kaam wala verb sentence ke end mein intezaar karta hai.
A modal verb adds a layer of meaning to another verb — ability, necessity, desire or a polite wish. Four to learn now:
wollen is a strong "want"; möchten is the polite "would like" — use möchten in cafés and shops. Both are everywhere in daily life.

Modal verb doosre verb ko matlab deta hai: können (sakna), müssen (karna hi padna), wollen (chahna), möchten (polite "chahunga"). Café/shop mein aksar möchten behtar lagta hai — "wollen" thoda seedha aur blunt sunai deta hai.
The sentence bracket — infinitive at the end
Modal in slot 2, infinitive at the very end. Everything else sits between them.

German builds a frame: you hear the modal early, so you know a second verb is coming, and the sentence stays open until that verb lands. This bracket is the same shape you will meet again in the Perfekt — helper early, second verb-part last.
Do verb hote hain aur dono alag-alag jagah baithte hain: modal position 2 par, aur infinitive sentence ke end mein. Beech mein baaki sab kuch aa jaata hai.
The second verb stays an infinitive and goes last.
This is the key structure. The modal takes position 2; the main verb becomes an infinitive and goes to the very END. Together they "bracket" the sentence (die Satzklammer).
Only ONE verb is conjugated — the modal. The other stays in its dictionary (infinitive) form and waits at the end. Everything else sits in the middle.

Yeh sabse zaroori structure hai: modal position 2 pe, aur main verb infinitive ban kar bilkul END mein. Sirf ek verb conjugate hota hai (modal); doosra apni dictionary form mein end pe rukta hai. Ise Satzklammer kehte hain.
ich and er/sie/es are identical and take no ending — and the singular changes its vowel.
Modal ka singular bilkul plain hota hai — koi ending nahi: ich kann, er kann. Aur vowel badal jaata hai: können → kann.
These three share a pattern: the ich and er/sie/es forms have no ending and a changed stem vowel.
Notice ich and er/sie/es are identical (kann/kann, muss/muss, will/will) — no -e, no -t. The stem vowel changes in the singular: können→kann, müssen→muss, wollen→will.

Teeno ka pattern same: ich aur er/sie/es ek jaise hain (kann/kann) — koi ending nahi. Singular mein stem vowel badalta hai: können→kann, müssen→muss, wollen→will. Yaad rakho: ich kann, du kannst, er kann.
möchten is the polite favourite, and modals form questions just like any other verb.
ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte
For yes/no questions the modal goes FIRST: "Kannst du …?", "Müssen wir …?". For W-Fragen the modal stays in position 2. The infinitive still waits at the end.

möchten polite hai: ich möchte, du möchtest. Ja/Nein sawaal mein modal sabse pehle: "Kannst du mir helfen?". W-Frage mein modal position 2 pe: "Was möchtest du trinken?". Infinitive phir bhi end mein rukta hai.
The infinitive goes to the very end, after the object.
No "zu" after a modal — just the plain infinitive.
ich-form of können has no ending: kann, not kanne.
Only the modal is conjugated; the main verb stays infinitive at the end.

Char galtiyan common hain. Infinitive sentence ke end mein aata hai, object ke baad: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen. Modal ke baad zu nahi lagta: Ich will lernen. ich-form par koi ending nahi lagti: kann, na ki “kanne”. Aur sirf modal conjugate hota hai — main verb end mein infinitive ban kar rehta hai: Ich muss heute lernen.
Modal position 2 after front time word (this chapter).
We want to have a party.
Max wants to do the music.
Modal position 2 after front adverb (this chapter).
Everyone would like to eat pizza.

On Saturday Anna and Max want to have a party. Max wants to do the music. Rohan must do his homework first. Afterwards he can come. Everyone would like to eat pizza. Hopefully the party will be great!
Finn, willst du morgen zusammen lernen?
Finn, do you want to study together tomorrow?
Ich muss zuerst arbeiten, aber danach kann ich kommen.
I have to work first, but afterwards I can come.
Gut, wir wollen um vier anfangen.
Good, we want to start at four.
Ja, aber er muss sein eigenes Buch mitbringen!

A separable verb is built from a small prefix + a base verb: auf + stehen = aufstehen (to get up). In the dictionary it’s one word — but in a sentence it splits.
The prefix usually carries the meaning. The same base verb takes many prefixes: anmachen (turn on) vs ausmachen (turn off) vs aufmachen (open) vs zumachen (close).
Separable verb = chhota prefix + base verb: auf + stehen = aufstehen (uthna). Dictionary mein ek shabd, par sentence mein alag. Prefix hi matlab badalta hai: anmachen (chaalu) vs ausmachen (band).
The split: prefix flies to the end
Conjugated part in slot 2, prefix at the very end. Everything else in between.
aufstehen → Ich stehe um sechs auf.
Prefix ko sentence ke end mein bhejo. Yeh wahi bracket hai jo modal mein tha — shuru mein ek hissa, sentence ke end mein doosra.
Question: verb first, prefix still last.
After a modal the verb stays whole at the end.
In a normal statement, the verb is conjugated in position 2 and the prefix breaks off and goes to the very end. The two halves form a bracket around the sentence.
The conjugated stem stays in position 2; the prefix waits at the end. Everything else (time, object) sits in between. Don’t leave them stuck together: NOT "Ich aufstehe …".

Statement mein verb position 2 par conjugate hota hai, aur prefix tootkar sentence ke end mein chala jaata hai. Beech mein time aur object aa jaate hain. Dono ko saath rakhna galat hai — Ich aufstehe nahi, balki Ich stehe … auf.
In questions the verb moves but the prefix still waits at the end. After a modal verb (or in the infinitive), the separable verb stays whole.
Kommst du mit? (verb first, prefix end)
Yes/no question: verb first, prefix at the end — "Rufst du an?". After a modal the main verb is an infinitive at the end and stays joined: "Ich will einkaufen." Never split it there.
Sawaal mein bhi prefix end mein hi rehta hai: Kommst du mit? Lekin modal ke baad verb poora rehta hai aur infinitive ban kar end mein jaata hai: Ich muss aufstehen. Wahaan use todna nahi hai.
Stress the prefix → it splits. Cannot stress it → it never splits.

You can hear the difference before you know the rule. AUFstehen puts the weight on the prefix, so the prefix is a real word and can stand alone at the end. In beGINnen the weight is on the stem, so be- is not a word and has nothing to stand on.
Prefix par zor hai? Alag ho jaayega. Zor stem par hai? Chipka rahega.
Some prefixes never separate. The inseparable ones (be-, ver-, er-, ent-, ge-) stay glued; the separable ones (auf-, an-, ein-, mit-, ab-, aus-, zu-, los-…) break off.
Stressed prefix (AUFstehen) = separable. Unstressed prefix (be-, ver-, er-, ent-) = inseparable, e.g. beginnen never splits. When you learn a verb, learn whether the prefix splits.

Pehchanne ka simple tarika yeh hai ki zor kahaan pad raha hai. Agar prefix par zor hai, jaise AUFstehen, to woh separable hai. Aur jin prefixes par zor nahi padta (be-, ver-, er-, ent-), woh inseparable hote hain — jaise beginnen, jo kabhi nahi tootta. Isliye naya verb seekhte waqt yeh bhi note kar lo ki uska prefix alag hota hai ya nahi.
Split it: verb in position 2, prefix at the end.
The prefix goes after the object, at the very end.
After a modal the verb stays a whole infinitive.
Don’t drop the prefix — mitkommen needs its mit.

Char galtiyan dhyaan mein rakho. Verb ko todna zaroori hai: Ich stehe … auf, na ki Ich aufstehe. Prefix object ke baad, sentence ke end mein aata hai: Ich rufe dich an. Modal ke baad verb poora rehta hai: Ich muss aufstehen. Aur prefix ko girana nahi hai: Kommst du mit?
Am Samstag stehe ich spät auf.
On Saturday I get up late.

The numbers 0 to 12 have no pattern. You learn them the way you learned them in your own language — by saying them until they are automatic. Every other number in German is built out of these twelve, so this is the one list worth learning cold.
Say them in a rhythm rather than reading them off a page. klopfen (tap) the table as you go, the way you practised stress in Chapter 2.
Learn 0–12 by ear, not by sight. Everything above 12 is assembled from them.
Counting starts with eins, but directly before a noun it drops the -s: ein Buch, eine Frau. So "one book" is ein Buch, never eins Buch. Remember this — the reversal rule below needs it.

0 se 12 tak koi pattern nahi hai — inhe bas yaad karna padta hai, kyunki aage ke saare numbers inhi se bante hain. Kaagaz se padhne se better hai bol-bol kar rhythm mein yaad karo. Ek dhyaan ki baat: ginti mein eins, par noun se pehle sirf ein (ein Buch, eine Frau) — yeh baat neeche reversal rule mein kaam aayegi.
Do bhaag mein todo: null se sechs, phir sieben se zwölf. Chhe-chhe ka set aasaan baithta hai.
Every number here uses sounds you already have: z = "ts" (zwei = "tsvai", Chapter 1), ei = "eye" (drei, eins, Chapter 2), and ü = lips "u" + "ee" (fünf, zwölf).
The teens are assembled, not memorised: take the unit (3–9), stick -zehn (ten) on the end, and you are done. drei + zehn = dreizehn.
Only two of the seven change shape, and they change for the same reason: German trims a syllable that would be awkward to say.
unit + -zehn. Only sechzehn and siebzehn lose a piece.
Say sechszehn and siebenzehn out loud and you can hear the problem — too many consonants in a row, too many syllables. German shortened them centuries ago for exactly the reason you would.

Teens banane padte hain, ratne nahi: unit + -zehn (das). drei+zehn = dreizehn. Sirf do jagah shape badalta hai: sechzehn (s gir gaya) aur siebzehn (-en gir gaya). Wajah bhi simple hai — "sechszehn" aur "siebenzehn" bolna mushkil hai, isliye German ne chhota kar diya.
16 aur 17 chhote ho jaate hain, baaki teens poore rehte hain.
sechzehn drops the s; siebzehn drops the -en.
The other five are completely regular.
The tens work the same way as the teens, with a different ending: base number + -zig. vier → vierzig, fünf → fünfzig.
Two of them are irregular and simply have to be learned: zwanzig (20) and dreißig (30). And the same two numbers that shortened in the teens shorten again here.
base + -zig. Except zwanzig, and dreißig which is spelled with ß.
sechzig and siebzig shorten exactly as sechzehn and siebzehn did — same two numbers, same two cuts. Learn the pair once and it covers four words.

Tens bhi bante hain: base + -zig (vier → vierzig). Do irregular hain: zwanzig (20) aur dreißig (30 — ß ke saath, -zig nahi). Aur wahi do numbers phir chhote hote hain: sechzig, siebzig — bilkul jaise 16 aur 17 mein hua tha. Ek hi baat do jagah kaam aa gayi. 100 = hundert.
Teens ka -zehn, tens ka -zig. Aur "chhota hone wale" numbers wahi do hain: sechs aur sieben.
zwanzig and dreißig are irregular; dreißig takes ß.
The ending -zig is said "tsikh", not "tsig" — that is Chapter 2's rule that word-final -ig becomes "ikh". So zwanzig = "TSVAN-tsikh".
The reversal rule — units before tens
This is the heart of German numbers. For 21–99 you say the unit first, then und, then the ten — and you write the whole thing as one word. einundzwanzig is literally "one-and-twenty".
English does this too, in old poetry and in "four and twenty blackbirds". German simply never stopped.
Small number first, then und, then the big one — one word, no spaces.

Reading a two-digit German number out loud means holding the second digit in your head first. This feels backwards for about a week, then it stops being an effort. The fastest way through is saying prices and house numbers aloud, not translating them.

Two details in that table are worth naming. Before und, 1 is ein, never eins. And sechs and sieben stay full in front of und — they only shorten when they carry -zehn or -zig. So 67 is sieben-und-sechzig: the first seven is whole, the sixty is clipped.

Shuru mein ulta lagega, kuch din baad normal ho jaayega — bas prices aur ghar ke number bol-bol kar practice karo, translate mat karo. Do baat yaad rakho: und se pehle 1 = ein (eins nahi), aur sechs/sieben und ke aage poore rehte hain — woh sirf -zehn/-zig ke saath chhote hote hain.
Chhota number pehle, bada baad mein. Ulta bolo, ek word mein likho.
21–99: unit + und + ten, written as one word.

Numbers at work — age, prices, phone numbers
Knowing the numbers is not the same as using them. Three everyday jobs cover almost everything you will need at A1, and each has a fixed pattern you can copy exactly.
Age uses the verb sein (to be), not "have" — this is the opposite of Hindi and of several other languages, so it is worth fixing early.
Age: Ich bin … Jahre alt. Price: Das kostet … Euro. Phone number: read it digit by digit.
Ich bin einundzwanzig Jahre alt. → age
Wie alt bist du? → asking age
null, eins, sieben, vier, neun, zwei

After a number, Euro and Jahre do not take an English-style plural -s: fünfzehn Euro, not Euros. And a phone number is never said as a big number — Germans read the digits, sometimes in pairs, never "seventeen thousand four hundred".
German counts Jahre as a measurement, and measurement words after a number stay in their plain form — the number already tells you how many, so the word does not need to repeat it.

Numbers aa gaye, ab dekho inka kaam kya hai. Teen cheezein lagbhag sab kuch cover kar deti hain. Pehli, umar batana — German mein hona use hota hai, rakhna nahi: Ich bin einundzwanzig Jahre alt, matlab "main ikkees saal ka hoon". Yeh Hindi se ulta hai. Poochhne ke liye Wie alt bist du? aata hai. Doosri, daam batana: Das kostet fünfzehn Euro — aur number ke baad Euro waise hi rehta hai, "Euros" nahi. Teesri, phone number — usme ek-ek digit padha jaata hai (null, eins, sieben…), poora number ek saath nahi bola jaata.
Umar ke liye bin (hoon), habe nahi. Aur number ke baad Euro hamesha akela — "s" nahi lagta.
Age = Ich bin … Jahre alt. (sein, not haben)
Price = … kostet … Euro. — Euro never takes an -s.
Phone numbers are read digit by digit.
Four habits account for nearly every number mistake at this level. Three are spelling, one is word order — and the word-order one is the only one that stops you being understood.
Each row below is a rule from this chapter, seen from the wrong side.
Unit first, then und, then the ten — and always one word. This is the mistake that actually confuses a listener.
sechs drops its s before -zehn and -zig. Same for sieben → siebzehn, siebzig.
Thirty is the one ten spelled with ß. Every other ten uses -zig.
German is an age, it does not have one: sein + Jahre alt. And keep the word alt — without it the sentence is incomplete.

Chaar galtiyan se bachna hai. Pehli, 21 ko einundzwanzig likhna — order ulta hota hai aur sab ek hi shabd mein aata hai. Yahi ek galti hai jo samajhne mein sach mein rukaawat daalti hai. Doosri, 16 sechzehn hai, jisme s gir jaata hai. Teesri, 30 dreißig hai, ß ke saath. Aur chauthi, umar ke liye Ich bin … Jahre alt aata hai — habe nahi, aur alt chhodna nahi hai.
Chaar check: order ulta hai? sechs/sieben chhote hue? dreißig mein ß? umar mein bin … alt?

Use sein for change of state

Same frame as before — only the helper changes. sein in slot 2, participle at the end.

Same frame as the haben-Perfekt — just a different helper. sein is conjugated and sits in position 2; the Partizip II goes to the very end.
Conjugate sein: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir/sie/Sie sind, ihr seid. The participle never changes — exactly like the haben-Perfekt, just the helper is different.
Wahi frame, sirf helper alag: sein conjugate (ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid) position 2 pe + Partizip II end mein. Participle nahi badalta.
The biggest group: verbs that move you from one place to another (a change of location, Ortsveränderung).
Going, driving, flying, coming, travelling, running, walking — all movement A → B → sein. The separable ones split: ankommen → angekommen, abfahren → abgefahren, losfahren → losgefahren.
Jaana, gaadi, udna, aana, ghoomna, daudna — sab movement A→B → sein. Separable wale tootte hain: ankommen → angekommen, abfahren → abgefahren.
Which verbs take sein? (change & two specials)
The second group: verbs of change of state. Plus two important exceptions that have no movement at all.
Change of state (becoming different): aufstehen, einschlafen, aufwachen, werden → sein. And memorise the two odd ones with no movement: sein (gewesen) and bleiben (geblieben).
Change of state (badalna): aufstehen, einschlafen, aufwachen, werden → sein. Aur do bina-movement wale yaad karo: sein (gewesen) aur bleiben (geblieben).
Did the subject change place or change state? → sein. Everything else → haben.
Ek sawaal: subject khud hila ya badla? Haan → sein. Nahi → haben.
sein and bleiben are the two to memorise.

The participle goes to the very end.

A verb’s prefix decides what happens to the ge- in its participle. Separable prefixes (an-, auf-, ein-, mit-, zurück-) slot ge- into the middle: anrufen → angerufen. Inseparable prefixes (be-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp-, ge-) take no ge- at all: bekommen → bekommen, erklären → erklärt.

weil ke baad verb apni seat chhod kar aakhri seat le leta hai. weil = verb ko last seat milti hai.
weil → conjugated verb at the end of its clause.
A comma always comes before weil.
denn means the same but keeps normal order.
After weil, everything shifts: subject first, then the rest, and the conjugated verb lands at the very end of the clause.
In the weil-clause the verb is last: "weil ich müde bin", "weil ich Zeit habe". A comma always comes before weil. This "verb to the end" rule is the single most important point of the chapter.

weil ke baad pehle subject aata hai, phir baaki cheezein, aur conjugated verb sentence ke end mein chala jaata hai: weil ich müde bin, weil ich Zeit habe. weil se pehle comma lagana zaroori hai. Yeh verb-end-mein wala rule A1 ka sabse important rule hai.
deshalb takes slot 1, so the verb lands in slot 2 — before the subject.
Reason = weil / denn. Result = deshalb. Aur deshalb slot 1 le leta hai, isliye verb subject se pehle.
deshalb (therefore/so) shows a result. It is an adverb, so it takes position 1 — which pushes the verb in front of the subject.
Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
It’s raining, so I stay home.
Ich bin müde, deshalb gehe ich nicht.
I’m tired, so I’m not going.
After deshalb the verb comes next (position 2), before the subject: "deshalb bleibe ich …". also works the same way. Cause = weil/denn; result = deshalb/also.

deshalb ka matlab “isliye” hai aur yeh result batata hai. Yeh position 1 le leta hai, isliye verb subject se pehle aa jaata hai: deshalb bleibe ich …. also bhi isi tarah kaam karta hai. Simple tarika yeh hai: reason batana ho to weil ya denn, aur result batana ho to deshalb.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich bin krank.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
After weil the verb goes to the very end: … krank bin.
Es regnet, deshalb ich bleibe zu Hause.
Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
After deshalb the verb comes before the subject.

Ich lerne und ich bin müde aber.

aber joins clauses at the front, not the end.

German uses the case to carry information English carries with different words. "in the kitchen" and "into the kitchen" are two prepositions in English; in German it is one preposition and the article tells you which one you meant.

A single question decides the case. Is there movement toward a goal (Wohin? = where to?) or just a location (Wo? = where?)

Greetings — by the time of day
German picks its greeting by the clock. There is no single all-purpose "hello" that is also polite — so you choose by the hour, and the choice is part of being polite.
Hallo is the exception: it works almost anytime and with almost anyone, but it stays friendly rather than formal. The "Guten …" greetings are the polite set.
Regional hellos exist too, and Germans use them constantly: Moin in the north, Grüß Gott in the south and Austria, Grüezi in Switzerland. You do not have to say them, but you should recognise them.
Morning · day · evening → Guten Morgen · Guten Tag · Guten Abend. Unsure of the hour? Guten Tag.

Two things to store as-is. Gute Nacht is not a hello — it is only said last thing at night before sleeping. And notice it is Gute Nacht but Guten Tag: the ending changes with the noun. You do not need the reason yet — learn all four as fixed phrases and you will never write Guten Nacht.

German mein greeting ghadi dekh kar chunte hain — koi ek "hello" nahi jo har waqt polite bhi ho. Hallo kabhi bhi chalega, par woh dostana hai, formal nahi. Guten Morgen (subah), Guten Tag (din — sabse safe), Guten Abend (shaam). Gute Nacht sirf sone jaate waqt — yeh hello nahi hai. Aur dhyaan do: Gute Nacht par Guten Tag — ending badal jaati hai. Wajah baad ke chapter mein aayegi; abhi chaaron ko poore phrase ki tarah yaad rakho.

Greet by the hour: Morgen / Tag / Abend.
Hallo is friendly and always safe; Guten Tag is polite and always safe.

Goodbyes split the same way greetings do: one formal, several casual. Getting this wrong is more noticeable than getting a greeting wrong, because the goodbye is the last thing the other person hears.
Auf Wiedersehen is the full, formal goodbye. Everything else on this list is friendly.
Formal = Auf Wiedersehen. Friendly = Tschüs and the bis … family.

bis means "until", so the whole family is literally a promise about time: bis bald = "until soon", bis später = "until later", bis morgen = "until tomorrow". Once you see that, you can build new ones yourself.

Tschüs, Ciao = casual. Bis … ka matlab "… tak" hai, isliye yeh poora family time ka vaada hai: bis bald (jald tak), bis später (baad tak), bis morgen (kal tak) — matlab tum khud naye bana sakte ho.

Wie alt bist du? (How old are you?)

Origin always uses aus + the place, for countries and cities alike: Ich komme aus Indien, Ich komme aus Delhi. If you live somewhere different from where you are from, that is wohnen in: Ich wohne in Berlin.

Formal vs informal — du or Sie
German has two words for "you", and choosing between them is the single most visible politeness decision you make. du is for friends, family and children. Sie is for everyone else.
And the choice does more than swap one word: the verb ending changes with it. That is why the same question looks different in the two columns below.
du → verb ends in -st. Sie → verb ends in -en, and Sie is always capitalised.
du → du kommst, du wohnst, du bist
Sie → Sie kommen, Sie wohnen, Sie sind
and: ich → ich komme, ich wohne, ich bin

One small adjustment, visible in this chapter's own dialogue: when a verb stem already ends in an s-sound (-s, -ß, -z), the du ending drops to just -t, because -sst is unsayable. So it is du heißt, not du heißst. Same rule, one letter fewer.Pick one register at the start of a conversation and stay in it. Mixing Sie and du with the same person in the same conversation is the mistake Germans notice most — more than a wrong ending. When in doubt, choose Sie: it is never rude to be too polite, and the other person will offer you du when they want it.

The polite Sie is really the "they" form borrowed as a courtesy — that is why its verb ending is -en like a plural, and why it is written with a capital S even in the middle of a sentence. So you are not learning a new verb form here; you are borrowing one you will meet again.

German mein "you" ke do roop hain, aur yeh choice tumhari politeness ka sabse saaf signal hai. Doston, ghar walon aur bacchon ke saath du. Baaki sab ke saath Sie + Herr/Frau + surname. Sirf shabd nahi badalta — verb ka ending bhi badalta hai: du ke saath -st (du kommst), Sie ke saath -en (Sie kommen), aur ich ke saath -e (ich komme). Aur formal "aapka" = Ihr (Ihr Name), informal = dein. Ek chhoti baat: agar verb ka stem pehle se s/ß/z par khatam hota hai, to du ka ending sirf -t ban jaata hai — du heißt, kyunki "heißst" bola hi nahi jaa sakta. Sabse zaruri baat: ek conversation mein ek hi register — du aur Sie mix karna sabse zyada notice hota hai. Doubt ho to Sie; zyada polite hona kabhi galat nahi.

The ending follows the pronoun: du -st, Sie -en, ich -e.
After a stem ending in s / ß / z, du takes just -t: du heißt.
One register per conversation — never mix them.

Two contractions cover most of the calendar. am (= an dem) for days and parts of the day; im (= in dem) for months and seasons.
am = days & day-parts (am Freitag, am Abend) — but the one exception is in der Nacht. im = months & seasons (im Mai, im Sommer). Both are dative contractions (an dem → am, in dem → im).
am = din aur din ke hisse (am Freitag, am Abend) — sirf in der Nacht alag. im = mahina aur mausam (im Mai, im Sommer). Dono dative contractions hain (an dem → am, in dem → im).

seit = already going on (past → now). ab = starts from now onward.
seit peeche dekhta hai (do mahine se), ab aage dekhta hai (kal se). Dono dative lete hain.
seit says how long something has already been going on; ab marks a starting point in the future. Both take the dative.

A Personalpronomen is the small word that stands in for a person as the subject of a sentence — I, you, he, she. German has eight of them, and they matter more than in English, because the verb changes shape to match whichever one you pick.

Learn them as one block, in this order. Every verb table you meet from now on — in this chapter and every chapter after it — is printed in exactly this order, so the order itself becomes a memory aid.
Choose the pronoun first, then the verb follows it. Never the other way round.

Three of them look identical: sie = she, sie = they, and capital Sie = formal you. You never actually have to guess — the verb settles it. sie ist can only be "she is"; sie sind can only be "they are" or "you are". And formal Sie is capitalised wherever it stands in the sentence.
The three sie forms, told apart by the verb alone:

Personalpronomen = wo chhota word jo subject ki jagah aata hai. Aath yaad karo, aur isi order mein: ich (main), du (tum), er/sie/es (vah), wir (hum), ihr (tum sab), sie (ve), Sie (aap). Aage ke saare verb tables isi order mein aayenge, isliye order khud hi yaad rakhne mein madad karta hai. Teen roop ek jaise dikhte hain — sie=vah (stri), sie=ve, Sie=aap — par guess karne ki zarurat nahi: verb bata deta hai. sie ist = vah hai; sie sind = ve hain / aap hain.
Verb hi sie ka matlab kholta hai: ist = akeli (vah), sind = kai (ve/aap).
Eight pronouns, always learned in the same order.
The verb changes to match the pronoun — pronoun first, verb after.
sie ist = she is · sie sind = they are · Sie sind = you are (formal).
You already met three of these endings when choosing between du and Sie: ich -e, du -st, Sie -en. This chapter fills in the rest of the row.

German's most-used verb is sein (to be), and like English "to be" it is completely irregular — the forms do not look like the infinitive at all. That is not bad news: it means there are only six short words, and you already use their English equivalents without thinking.
You need this verb for almost everything in this chapter: who you are, where you are, how old you are, what you are.
Six forms, three of them the same word: bin · bist · ist · sind · seid · sind.

The whole table is really two groups. The b- forms are singular and personal: bin, bist. The s- forms are the rest: ist, sind, seid, sind. And three pronouns share one word — wir, sie and Sie all take sind, so learning that one form covers half the table.

Irregular verbs are irregular because they are old and used constantly — the same reason English kept "am / are / is" instead of regularising it. High use protects odd shapes. So the most irregular verb is also the one you will hear most often, which is exactly what makes it stick.

Par ghabrane ki baat nahi: sirf chhe chhote shabd hain, aur teen pronoun ek hi shabd share karte hain. Do group bana lo: b- wale singular aur personal hain (bin, bist), aur s- wale baaki sab (ist, sind, seid, sind). wir, sie aur Sie — teeno sind, matlab ek form se aadhi table cover ho gayi. Galti se bhi "ich bist" ya "du bin" nahi.

Other verbs: what er, sie and es do
Once you can talk about yourself, the next step is talking about someone. For ordinary verbs — not sein — the er / sie / es form simply adds -t to the stem.
You only need this one extra ending in this chapter, so that you can say what a third person does: Sie kommt aus Indien.
komm- : ich komme · du kommst · sie kommt
wohn- : ich wohne · du wohnst · er wohnt
but sein: ich bin · du bist · sie ist (irregular)
Notice heißen: du heißt and sie heißt come out identical, because a stem ending in ß cannot take -sst. Only the pronoun tells you which one is meant — one more reason German never drops the pronoun.

Apne baare mein bol liya, ab kisi aur ke baare mein. Aam verbs mein — sein ko chhod kar — er/sie/es ke saath sirf -t lagta hai: sie kommt, er wohnt, sie heißt. Poora pattern: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t. Ek dilchasp baat: heißen mein du heißt aur sie heißt ek jaise ban jaate hain — isliye pronoun girana kabhi possible nahi.
-e, -st, -t — main, tum, vah. Teen ending, teen log.
sein ignores this pattern entirely — it has its own six forms.

Word order: the verb is always second
German statements have one unbreakable habit: the Verb sits in second position. Not the second word — the second slot. Whatever fills the first slot, the verb comes straight after it.
This is the rule that makes German feel different from English, and it holds for the whole language. Get it now and dozens of later chapters cost you nothing.
One idea, then the verb, then everything else. The verb never moves from slot 2.
Mein Name | ist | Anna Klein. ← three words, still slot 1
Jetzt | wohne | ich in Berlin. ← subject moved to slot 3

Two things that trip people up. First, slot 1 can hold several words — Mein Name is three syllables and two words, but it is one idea, so it fills slot 1 and ist is still second. Second, slot 1 does not have to be the subject: put Jetzt first, as the Story does, and the subject slides behind the verb. The verb itself never moves.

German can shuffle almost everything else in the sentence, so it needs one fixed landmark for the listener. The verb is that landmark: hear the second slot and you know what is happening, no matter how the rest is arranged. Possessives are the one thing that never separate from their noun — mein Name, dein Vorname travel together as a unit.

German statement ka ek hi pakka rule hai: verb doosri jagah par aata hai. Dhyaan do ki yeh doosra shabd nahi, balki doosra slot hai. Pehle slot mein jo bhi daalo, verb turant uske baad aayega. Do cheezein log galat samajhte hain. Pehli, ki pehla slot ek se zyada shabd le sakta hai — Mein Name do shabd hain par ek hi idea hai, isliye ist phir bhi doosre slot par rehta hai. Doosri, ki pehle slot mein subject hona zaroori nahi — agar Jetzt aage rakh do to subject verb ke peeche chala jaata hai: Jetzt wohne ich in Berlin. Verb khud apni jagah nahi chhodta. Wajah simple hai: German baaki sab kuch idhar-udhar kar sakta hai, isliye sunne wale ko ek fixed point chahiye, aur wahi point verb hai.
Verb ki seat number 2 reserved hai. Pehli seat par kuch bhi baithe, verb apni seat nahi chhodta.
The verb is always in slot 2 of a statement.
Slot 1 is one idea, not one word — Mein Name counts as one.
If something else takes slot 1, the subject moves after the verb.
Chapter 6 (W-Fragen) uses this same slot rule for questions, and Chapter 19 (Satzposition) returns to it in full. Everything there is built on the sentence you just learned.
Four habits, and two of them come straight from Hindi sentence structure — which makes them easy to predict and easy to catch.
Each row is a rule from this chapter, seen from the wrong side.
The verb must match the pronoun: ich → bin, du → bist. Pick the pronoun first, then read its form off the table.
Hindi can drop "main"; German cannot drop "ich". The subject pronoun is compulsory in every statement.
Hindi puts the verb at the end. German puts it in slot 2 of a statement — that is the habit to rebuild.
Lower-case sie is "they"; capital Sie is the polite "you". In writing the capital is the only thing separating them.

Chaar galtiyan hoti hain, aur do seedhe Hindi ke structure se aati hain — isliye pehle se pata hai kahan sambhalna hai. Pehli, verb ko pronoun se match karna: ich bin sahi hai, "ich bist" nahi. Doosri, subject girana — Hindi mein "main" chhod sakte hain, par German mein ich nahi chhodte. Teesri, verb ko sentence ke end mein bhej dena — statement mein woh doosri jagah par rehta hai: Ich bin Anna, na ki "Ich Anna bin". Aur chauthi, likhte waqt Sie capital rakhna, kyunki chhota "sie" ka matlab "ve" ho jaata hai.

Up to now you have mostly been answering. A W-Frage lets you ask. It opens with a W-word and demands real information back — a name, a place, a reason. Yes or no is never an acceptable answer to one.

Every one of these words begins with the letter W, which is why Germans call them W-Wörter and the questions W-Fragen. That single letter is your signal: if a question starts with W, the answer must be information.
W-word at the front → the answer must be information, never ja or nein.

Two shapes of wie viel, and the difference is countability: wie viel for things you measure (Wie viel Zeit?, Wie viel kostet das?) and wie viele for things you count (Wie viele Bücher?). If you could put a number in front of it, use wie viele.

Ab tak tum zyada-tar jawaab de rahe the — W-Frage tumhe poochhna sikhati hai. Yeh W-Wort se shuru hota hai aur asli jaankari maangta hai: naam, jagah, wajah. Iska jawaab kabhi sirf "ja/nein" nahi ho sakta, aur yahi iski pehchaan hai. Wer? (kaun), Was? (kya), Wie? (kaise / naam), Wie viele? (kitne). Ek chhota farak: wie viel jo naapa jaata hai (Zeit, Geld), wie viele jo gina jaata hai (Bücher) — agar aage number lag sakta hai, to wie viele.
Sawaal W se shuru hua? To jawaab mein jaankari deni hai, sirf haan-naa nahi.
A W-Frage asks for information, not yes/no.
Wer = person · Was = thing · Wie = how or a name.
wie viel for measured amounts, wie viele for countable things.

Three W-words look almost identical and all deal with place — but they ask three different things, and each one pulls a different answer word after it. This trio is where beginners lose the most marks, so learn each question together with the word its answer needs.
The good news: the endings tell you the meaning. -her means motion from, -hin means motion to, and bare wo means no motion at all.
wo → in · woher → aus · wohin → nach. Question and answer word travel as a pair.

German marks direction on the question word itself, where English needs an extra word ("where from", "where to"). So German is doing you a favour: the information is packed into one short word, and you only have to hear the ending.

Teen jagah wale W-Wort lagbhag ek jaise dikhte hain, par teen alag cheezein poochhte hain — aur har ek apne saath ek khaas answer word maangta hai. Isliye sawaal aur jawaab ko jodi mein yaad karo: Wo? = kahaan (ek hi jagah) → in. Woher? = kahaan se → aus. Wohin? = kahaan ko → nach. Pehchaan ending se hoti hai: -her matlab kahin se aana, -hin matlab kahin ko jaana, aur akela wo matlab hilna hi nahi.
her = idhar (mere paas se aana), hin = udhar (wahan ko jaana). Akela wo = wahin khade raho.
Time, reason and duration: wann, warum, wie lange
Three more W-words, and between them they cover the questions you will be asked most often after your name: when something happens, why you are doing it, and how long you have been at it.
Both take completely ordinary answers — no special preposition to memorise, unlike the place trio.
Wann? asks for a point in time. Warum? asks for a reason. Wie lange? asks for a length of time.

A Warum? question can be answered with a short phrase — Für die Arbeit, Für mein Studium — and that is enough at this level. A full "because …" sentence needs weil, which changes the word order; you will meet it later. You will hear it in this chapter's Listening, so recognise it, but you do not have to produce it yet.

Teen aur W-Wort, aur naam ke baad sabse zyada yahi poochhe jaate hain: kab, kyun aur kitne samay se. Achhi baat: inke jawaab mein koi khaas preposition yaad nahi karna padta — place wale teen ki tarah nahi. Wann? ka jawaab time hota hai (Um acht, Morgen — Chapter 3 ke numbers yahan kaam aayenge). Warum? ka jawaab is level par ek chhota phrase bhi kaafi hai: Für die Arbeit. Wie lange? ka jawaab ek duration: Sechs Monate. Poora "kyunki…" wala jawaab weil se banta hai, jo word order badal deta hai — woh baad mein aayega. Listening mein sunoge, samajh lo, par abhi bolna zaruri nahi.
Wann mein "n" hai jaise "number par time". Warum ka jawaab hamesha ek wajah.
Wann? → a time. Warum? → a reason. Wie lange? → a duration.
A short phrase answers Warum? perfectly at A1.
None of the three needs a special answer preposition.
Answering Wann? is where your numbers earn their keep — Um acht, Um neun. And welcher / welche / welches ("which one?") gets its own chapter later, once you know the articles from Chapter 10.
Word order: verb in second position
This is the rule that decides whether your question is right or wrong. The W-word takes the first slot, the verb takes the second, and the subject follows the verb.
You already know this rule — it is the verb-second habit from Chapter 5. Nothing new is happening; the W-word has simply moved into the slot that Jetzt or Ich used to occupy.
W-word, then verb, then subject. The verb never waits behind the subject.

One case looks like an exception and is not. When the W-word is itself the subject, there is no second subject to place: Wer kommt aus Indien?, Was ist das? The verb is still in slot 2 — slot 3 is simply empty, because wer and was are already doing that job. So never write Wer kommst du?

German lets you move almost everything else around, so the listener needs one fixed landmark to know what is happening. That landmark is the verb in slot 2 — in statements, in questions, everywhere. This is the single most valuable rule in the whole language.

Yeh rule tay karta hai ki tumhara sawaal sahi hai ya galat: W-Wort pehle, Verb doosre par, phir Subjekt. Yeh koi naya rule nahi — Chapter 5 ka wahi "verb doosri seat par" hai; bas pehli seat par ab W-Wort baith gaya hai. Galat: Woher du kommst? — Sahi: Woher kommst du? Ek case exception lagta hai par hai nahi: jab W-Wort khud subject ho, to doosra subject hi nahi hota — Wer kommt aus Indien?, Was ist das? Verb phir bhi doosri seat par hai. Isliye Wer kommst du? kabhi nahi.
Verb ki seat number 2 hai — statement ho ya sawaal, woh seat nahi badalti.
Never Woher du kommst? — the subject cannot jump the verb.
If the W-word is the subject, slot 3 is simply empty.
Exactly the rule you learned for statements: Jetzt wohne ich in Berlin. Statement or question, the verb stays in slot 2.
Four habits. Two are word order carried over from Hindi and English, two are picking the wrong W-word — and the wrong W-word is the one that gets you a useless answer.
Each row is a rule from this chapter, seen from the wrong side.
The verb must come second, straight after the W-word. Hindi and English both put the subject first here; German does not.
wo asks where you are, woher asks where you started. Ask wo and you will be told a place you already know.
wohnen has no movement in it, so it cannot take wohin. Movement verbs (gehen, fahren) take wohin; staying verbs take wo.
Zeit is measured, not counted, so it takes wie viel. Use wie viele only where a number could stand: wie viele Bücher.

Chaar galtiyan hoti hain. Do word order ki hain, jo Hindi aur English dono se aati hain, aur do galat W-Wort chunne ki — aur galat W-Wort ka result yeh hota hai ki jawaab bekaar mil jaata hai. Pehli, verb ko doosri seat par rakhna: Woher kommst du? sahi hai, "Woher du kommst?" nahi. Doosri, origin poochhne ke liye woher chahiye, sirf "wo" nahi. Teesri, wohnen mein koi movement nahi hai, isliye uske saath wohin nahi chalega — wahan wo aayega; movement wale verbs jaise gehen aur fahren ke saath wohin aata hai. Aur chauthi, wie viel un cheezon ke liye hai jo naapi jaati hain (Zeit, Geld), aur wie viele un ke liye jo gini jaati hain (Bücher).
Chaar check: verb slot 2 mein? sahi W-Wort? movement hai ya nahi? gin sakte ho ya naap sakte ho?
Chapter 7 (Ja oder Nein?) is the other half of asking. There the W-word disappears and the verb itself moves to slot 1 — which is exactly how German signals a yes/no question.
w = "v". "Wie heißt du?" asks for a name.
The verb sits second, right after the W-word. ß = sharp "ss".
Subject comes after the verb in a W-question.
The information asked for by "Wie heißt du?".
Asks for origin — answer with aus.
kommen for du: kommst — second position.
The answer to woher: aus + place.
Asks a static location — answer with in.
The answer to wo: in + place.

a1-7-jaodernein: Half of every conversation is a yes/no question. In German you make one by moving the verb to the front — no question word needed. Learn the verb-first pattern, the short answers, and how to say "not" with nicht.
To ask a yes/no question in German, just put the verb first: Kommst du aus Indien? The answer is Ja or Nein — and to make it negative you add nicht.
