Three sentence types — spot the difference
German changes the question by moving the verb, not by adding a word.
Verb doosri seat = keh raha hoon. Verb pehli seat = poochh raha hoon.
German has three everyday sentence shapes, and they differ only by where the verb goes. You already know the first two; this chapter adds the third.
The only thing that turns "Du sprichst Deutsch." into a question is moving sprichst to the front. No extra word needed.

German mein teen sentence — farak sirf verb kahan hai isme. Statement: verb doosre (Du sprichst …). W-Frage: W-Wort ke baad verb doosre. Ja-/Nein-Frage: verb sabse pehle (Sprichst du …?). Bas verb ko aage le aao — naya shabd nahi chahiye.
Making a yes/no question: verb first
Swap the first two words. That is the entire operation.

English needs a helper — "do you speak?" — because English verbs stopped being able to move to the front. German verbs never lost that ability, so German just moves the verb and needs no helper at all.
Subject aur verb ki jagah badal do: "Du kommst" → "Kommst du?" Kuch add nahi karna.
Statement = subject + verb. Yes/no question = verb + subject.
The intonation rises at the end.
Take any statement, move the verb to position 1, put the subject right after it, add a question mark — done.
It is the mirror image of a statement: statement = subject + verb; yes/no question = verb + subject.
Kisi bhi statement ka verb aage lao, subject uske baad, question mark lagao — ho gaya. "Du kommst …" → "Kommst du …?" Statement = subject+verb; yes/no question = verb+subject. Bilkul ulta.
A yes/no question is answered with Ja or Nein. You can stop there (short answer) or repeat the idea (full answer) to sound more natural.
Ja, ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch.
If you do not catch the question, say Entschuldigung? or Wie bitte? and ask them to repeat.

Jawaab Ja ya Nein se. Short answer (sirf "Ja.") theek hai, par full answer (idea dohra ke) zyada natural lagta hai: "Ja, ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch." Samajh na aaye to Entschuldigung? ya Wie bitte? bolo.
Negating the whole action → nicht at the end. Negating one word → nicht just before it.
Hindi mein "nahi" verb se pehle aata hai, par German mein nicht verb ke baad aata hai. Aur agar sirf ek word ko negate karna ho, to nicht us word se theek pehle rakho.
To make a sentence negative, add nicht (not). For now, two safe placements cover most A1 sentences.
nicht at the end (negates the verb)
nicht before the word it negates
No, I do not speak English.
A1 tip: to negate the whole action, nicht usually goes at the end. (To negate a noun with an article you use "kein" — that comes later.)

Negative banane ke liye nicht lagta hai, aur iski do safe jagah hain. Agar poori action negate karni ho to nicht aksar sentence ke end mein aata hai: Ich verstehe nicht. Aur agar kisi khaas shabd ko negate karna ho to nicht us shabd se pehle aata hai: Das ist nicht richtig. Noun ko negate karne ke liye kein use hota hai, jo aage ke chapter mein aayega.

Everything you ask is one of two shapes. The difference is just verb position.
W-Frage opens with a W-word (verb second); a yes/no question opens with the verb (verb first). Statements keep the verb second.

Do tarah ke sawaal hote hain, aur farak sirf verb ki jagah ka hai. W-Frage mein W-Wort pehle aata hai aur verb doosri jagah par: Woher kommst du? Aur Ja/Nein-Frage mein verb sabse pehle aata hai: Kommst du …? Jawaab Ja ya Nein se dete hain, aur negative banane ke liye nicht lagta hai.
Country and language are capitalised; the nationality adjective is lower-case.
Naam bade akshar se (Deutschland, Deutsch), par describe karne wala chhote se (deutsch). Aur zyada-tar desh ke saath article nahi — sirf kuch (die Türkei, die USA) lete hain.
Most countries take no article; die Türkei, die USA do.
The one new idea this chapter: keep three things apart — the country (a place), the language (capitalised), and the nationality adjective (lower-case).
Most countries take no article (aus Indien), but a few do: die Schweiz, die Türkei, die Ukraine, die USA, der Iran/Irak — these become aus der/den ….

Ek nayi cheez: teen alag rakho — desh (jagah), bhasha (capital: Deutsch), aur nationality adjective (chhota: deutsch). Zyadatar desh bina article (aus Indien), par kuch ke saath: die Schweiz/Türkei/USA, der Iran → "aus der/den …".
Four errors are the ones most likely to cost you points at A1 — two are spelling and capitalisation, two are choosing the wrong form.

The language is a noun — capitalise it. Lower-case deutsch is the adjective.
aus takes the dative: die Schweiz → der Schweiz.
Use a W-word for information; verb-first is only yes/no.
Lower-case sie is "they"; capital Sie is the polite "you". In writing the capital letter is the only thing telling them apart.

Chaar galtiyan A1 mein number kaat deti hain. Pehli, bhasha ka naam bade akshar se aata hai: Ich spreche Deutsch — chhota "deutsch" adjective hota hai. Doosri, aus der Schweiz sahi hai, kyunki aus ke baad Dativ aata hai. Teesri, origin poochhne ke liye Woher kommst du? chahiye, sirf "Kommst du?" nahi. Aur chauthi, sie, sie aur Sie ka farak yaad rakho — capital Sie ka matlab "aap" hota hai.

a1-9-verben: Verbs are the engine of every German sentence. Learn the everyday ones — arbeiten, lernen, machen, spielen, kochen — and the one regular pattern of present-tense endings that conjugates almost all of them across ich, du, er, wir, ihr, sie.

A German verb has two parts: a stem and an ending that changes with the subject. Take lernen → stem lern-, then add -e, -st, -t, -en. Learn that one pattern and you can use almost every everyday verb.

Which form does the verb have?
What is a verb? The infinitive
Cut -en off the infinitive and you have the stem. Everything you ever do to a German verb happens after that stem.
Infinitiv = stem + -en. Ulta karo: -en hatao, stem mil gaya.
A verb (Verb) is the action word — the engine of the sentence. Its base form, the one you find in a dictionary, is the Infinitiv.
Almost every German infinitive ends in -en (a few in just -n). Cut that off and what is left is the stem — the part you build on.
Infinitive = stem + -en — with a small group ending in just -n (sammeln → stem sammel-). For regular verbs the stem never changes; only the ending does.

Verb action word hai — sentence ka engine. Dictionary wala base form = Infinitiv, jo aksar -en par khatam hota hai (lernen, machen). -en hatao to bachta hai stem (lern-, mach-). Regular verbs mein stem nahi badalta, sirf ending badalti hai.
ich -e · du -st · er/sie/es -t · wir -en · ihr -t · sie/Sie -en.

English has almost given up on endings — only "he walks" survives. German kept the full set, and that is why German can move words around so freely: the ending already tells you who is doing it, so the word order is free to do other work.
stem + ending → lern- + e = ich lerne
Do endings do baar aate hain: -en (wir, sie/Sie) aur -t (er, ihr). Matlab chhe forms mein sirf chaar shabd yaad karne hain.
One ending set covers almost every regular verb.
wir and sie/Sie look exactly like the infinitive.
To use a verb, add the ending that matches the subject to the stem. This single set of endings works for almost every regular verb — learn it once.
Notice wir and sie/Sie are identical to the infinitive (-en). du = -st, er/sie/es and ihr = -t.

Verb use karne ke liye subject ke hisaab se ending lagao: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. Ek hi set lagbhag har regular verb par chalta hai. Dhyaan: wir aur sie/Sie infinitive jaise hi (-en) hain.
Spelling helper: stems ending in -t or -d
Stem ends in -t or -d? Slip an -e- in before the du, er and ihr endings.
This is not grammar, it is your mouth. Say "arbeitst" or "findst" out loud and you will hear why German refuses — the extra -e- exists purely so the word remains sayable.
Do consonant takra rahe hain? Beech mein ek -e- daal do.
If the stem already ends in -t or -d, the du, er/sie/es and ihr forms add an extra -e- so you can actually pronounce them.
Without the helper -e, "arbeitst" and "findst" would be unsayable — try them out loud. The rule applies only to stems ending in -t or -d; a normal stem like spiel- takes the plain endings.
Agar stem -t ya -d par khatam ho (jaise arbeit-), to du/er/ihr mein ek extra -e- aata hai: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. Warna "arbeitst" bola hi nahi jaata. Yeh rule sirf -t/-d wale stems par.
Word order: verb in second position
Whatever fills slot 1, the verb is slot 2 — and the subject moves out of the way if it has to.
Verb ki seat number 2 reserved hai. Time word aage aaya to subject peeche khisak jaata hai.
Statement = the verb sits second, always.
Front a time word and you get verb–subject: Morgen arbeite ich.
Slot 1 is one idea, not one word.

In a statement the conjugated verb stays in second position — the same rule from Chapter 5. If a time word like morgen or am Wochenende comes first, the verb still sits second and the subject jumps behind it.
When a time word opens the sentence, you get verb–subject: Morgen arbeite ich (not "Morgen ich arbeite").

Normal statement (Hauptsatz) mein verb doosri position par hota hai (Chapter 5 wala rule). Agar time word pehle aaye (morgen, am Wochenende), to verb phir bhi doosre, aur subject uske peeche: Morgen arbeite ich — "Morgen ich arbeite" nahi.
Four habits, and every one of them is about the ending rather than the word. Get the ending right and the rest of the verb takes care of itself.
Each row is a rule from this chapter, seen from the wrong side.
The ending must match the subject: ich -e, du -st.
The verb stays second; the subject moves after it.
The -en form is the infinitive (the dictionary form). It belongs to wir and sie/Sie, never to ich.

Char galtiyan common hain. Pehli, ending subject se match nahi karna — sahi hai ich lerne aur du lernst. Doosri, jin stems ke end mein -t ya -d hai, unme extra -e- bhool jaana: du arbeitest. Teesri, time word aage hone par verb ko doosri jagah par na rakhna: Morgen arbeite ich. Aur chauthi, infinitive aur conjugated form ko mix kar dena.
Time phrase — opens the sentence, so verb comes next.
Time word first → verb second, then subject.
Subject jumps behind the verb because the time word is first.
